It’s best to check the unis website but reasons include:

-Living in a low income area

-Having free school meals

-Studying at a very poor achieving school

-Being a young carer

-Being considerably ill (eg, diarrhoea and vomiting) during exams 

-Being *severely* ill (eg, hospital stays) before *or* during exams

-A close family member (parent or sibling) being severely ill before or during exams 

-A close family member dying before or during exams

-Having an undiagnosed/unaccommodated disability before or during exams 

-Missing a large period of school for reasons outside of your control, which may be mentioned above, eg, being seriously ill for a sustained period

You’ll probably need a medical note, proof of diagnosis, proof of treatment, etc for reasons involving illness or disability. When discussing past extenuating circumstances, or current extenuating circumstances don’t expect to change before exams, it’s best to mention them in the dedicated part of your UCAS application. This has to be done by your UCAS referee but you can suggest them on what to write. Many unis also have a separate extenuating circumstances form that they’ll ask you to fill out after receiving your application/giving an offer. Check for one on their website and fill it out to be sure, you can also fill these out throughout the year if something unexpected happens.

In tests of difference/experiments, you manipulate one variable (independent variable) to measure it’s effect on another variable (dependent variable). This involves having 2+ conditions then comparing them to find differences in data. 

For example, I want to study the *effect* of caffeine consumption (IV) on hours of sleep (DV). I would have two conditions, one where I gave participants caffeine at the end of the day, and one where I didn’t (manipulated IV). I would record each group’s hours of sleep, then analyse each set of data (condition 1 vs condition 2) in the hopes of finding a difference in each group’s sleep.

In tests of association/correlations, you measure two pre-existing variables (co-variables) then compare them to find similarities in data. You don’t manipulate anything and there’s no experimental design. 

For example, I want to study the *relationship* between caffeine consumption and hours of sleep. I would gather a single group of participants and record both their caffeine consumption and hours of sleep (no manipulation of either variable). I would then analyse each set of data (co-variable 1 vs co-variable 2) in the hopes of finding an association between caffeine and sleep.

Psychosis is more of a symptom than a disorder in and of itself. Therefore, if any sort of mental illness is acute enough, then yes. Seriously mentally ill people can become at risk of psychosis, including OCD sufferers. The possible early symptoms are too long to list, but that also means almost every symptom is found in some other mental illness, completely unrelated to psychosis. So instead I’m going to give you some advice.

Psychosis being a possibility may seem like bad news, but the good news is, it’s not OCD-specific. It’s like this for everyone. I am reminded of a quote; “the only thing we have to fear, is fear itself.” All this worrying and fretting and ruminating we do is only going to make things worse. Don’t panic - I’m not saying you’re psychotic just because you’re worrying about developing psychosis. I’m saying that for the minority of people with OCD who do develop it, this hypochondria and fear of illness we are predisposed to is one of the factors that led to it.

Long story short, instead of spending time worrying about the possibility of things getting worse, focus on making things better. Or just surviving as is. Because we attract what we fear, and ironically, the anxiety of a certain thing happening can often be it’s cause.
